blocks.text: Quick verdict

Infatica is a good NetNut replacement for compliance-conscious teams: it states that it does not resell IPs, holds ISO certifications, and its sourcing story directly addresses the concern that brought NetNut down. Practically, it offers ZIP targeting on every plan, SOCKS5, static ISP proxies for former NetNut static-residential users, and a $4 seven-day trial. Its 35M-40M pool is smaller than NetNut used to advertise, so test your key countries before moving everything.

Since July 2026, when the FBI seized NetNut's domains after Google tied its residential network to the Popa botnet, NetNut vs Infatica has become a migration question. Infatica is one of the providers most often considered by former NetNut customers who care about sourcing, because it publishes a no-reselling policy and ISO certifications. This page explains NetNut's status, compares Infatica with NetNut's former offer, and lists the steps to switch.
What happened to NetNut?

On July 2, 2026, the FBI, working with IRS Criminal Investigation, Google, Lumen and the Shadowserver Foundation, seized hundreds of domains tied to NetNut, the residential proxy service owned by Nasdaq-listed Alarum Technologies. Google's Threat Intelligence Group said NetNut's exit-node pool overlapped with Popa, a botnet it estimated at about two million consumer devices, many of them smart TVs and streaming boxes. Alarum disputes the botnet label and said it would cooperate with law enforcement, but netnut.com and, within days, netnut.io displayed federal seizure notices. As of October 2026 the service is not something you can responsibly buy or rely on.

blocks.text: Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica is a web-data provider with offices in the UK, Singapore and the UAE. It started with premium residential proxies and now sells mobile, static ISP, datacenter and IPv6 residential networks plus scraper APIs and datasets. Its residential pool is advertised at 35M-40M IPs in 195 countries, with ZIP-level targeting on every plan, and the company is unusually explicit about sourcing: it says it does not resell IPs and lists several ISO certifications.

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
What NetNut offered, and how Infatica compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Infatica covers much of the same ground: mobile, static isp, datacenter, ipv6 residential, scraper apis, datasets sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 35M-40M IPs in 195 countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Infatica
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Infatica's answer is yes; its other products are mobile, static ISP, datacenter, IPv6 residential, scraper APIs, datasets. On rotating residential targeting, Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP in 195 countries, with per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. On billing, Infatica uses pay-as-you-go or monthly subscription, and unused traffic is handled as follows: subscription traffic resets monthly. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Infatica pricing

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Quick cost check for Infatica: 10 GB comes to $40 (PAYG at $4/GB), and 100 GB comes to $360 (100 GB plan, $3.60/GB). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Infatica
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Infatica's targeting (country, state, city and ZIP).
2. Test before you commit. Infatica's testing option: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Infatica supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Infatica fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests.
SERP and rank tracking: strong fit. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results.
Social media and multi-account management: workable. Why: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: ZIP-level targeting for local prices.
Ad verification and geo-testing: strong fit. Why: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing.
Tight budgets: workable. Why: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Protocols and sessions

Infatica supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Targeting covers country, state, city and ZIP across 195 countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Infatica included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers and location-precise collection that needs ZIP targeting, starts at $4/GB pay-as-you-go, and offers 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
